description: Comprehensive question bank on Direct and Indirect Speech based on FDA & SDA Competitive Examination Notes. Covers definitions, rules, tense changes, pronoun changes, time/place expressions, all sentence types, reporting verbs, common errors, and practice questions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is direct speech?

options.A: Reporting the meaning of someone's words without quoting the exact words
options.B: Reporting the exact words spoken by a person, usually within quotation marks
options.C: A verb that introduces the reported words
options.D: The clause containing the words or meaning being reported

questions.explanation: Direct speech reports the exact words spoken by a person, usually within quotation marks: He said, "I am busy."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is indirect speech?

options.A: Reporting the exact words spoken by a person within quotation marks
options.B: A clause that identifies the speaker or reporting act
options.C: Reporting the meaning of someone's words without quoting the exact words
options.D: The exact words spoken by a person

questions.explanation: Indirect speech reports the meaning of someone's words without quoting the exact words: He said that he was busy.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is another name for indirect speech?

options.B: Reported speech
options.C: Quoted speech

questions.explanation: Reported speech is another name for indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a reporting verb?

options.A: A verb that introduces the reported words
options.B: The clause containing the words being reported
options.C: The exact words spoken by a person
options.D: A clause that identifies the speaker

questions.explanation: A reporting verb introduces the reported words, such as say, tell, ask, reply, explain, request, order, advise and suggest.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a reporting clause?

options.A: The clause containing the words or meaning being reported
options.B: The clause that identifies the speaker or reporting act
options.C: The exact words spoken by a person
options.D: A verb that introduces the reported words

questions.explanation: The reporting clause identifies the speaker or reporting act: "She said," "The teacher asked me," "He explained."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is a reported clause?

options.A: The clause that identifies the speaker or reporting act
options.B: A verb that introduces the reported words
options.C: The clause containing the words or meaning being reported
options.D: The exact words spoken by a person

questions.explanation: The reported clause contains the words or meaning being reported: "that she was tired" in "She said that she was tired."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the main difference between direct and indirect speech?

options.A: Direct speech uses quotation marks; indirect speech does not
options.B: Direct speech reports meaning; indirect speech reports exact words
options.C: Direct speech gives exact words; indirect speech reports content and adjusts grammar
options.D: Direct speech is always past tense; indirect speech is always present tense

questions.explanation: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words; indirect speech reports the content and adjusts grammar as required.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What punctuation is used in direct speech?

options.B: Quotation marks
options.C: Semicolons

questions.explanation: Quotation marks are used around the exact spoken words in direct speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Are quotation marks used in indirect speech?

options.B: Only for questions
options.C: No, normally not

questions.explanation: Indirect speech normally does not use quotation marks around the reported clause.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What are the main changes in converting direct speech into indirect speech?

options.B: Only pronoun changes
options.C: Reporting verb, tense, pronouns, possessive forms, demonstratives, time/place expressions, word order and punctuation

questions.explanation: Depending on context: reporting verb, tense, pronouns, possessive forms, demonstratives, time/place expressions, word order and punctuation all may change.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does every sentence require a tense change in indirect speech?

options.B: No, not for universal truths, continuing facts, or information that remains true
options.C: Only for questions

questions.explanation: Tense backshift is common when the reporting verb is in the past, but it is not compulsory for universal truths, continuing facts or information that remains true or relevant.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is backshift?

options.B: The usual movement of the reported verb to a past form when the reporting verb is in the past
options.C: Changing time and place expressions

questions.explanation: Backshift is the usual movement of the reported verb to a past form when the reporting verb is in the past: present simple → past simple; present perfect → past perfect.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to quotation marks when converting to indirect speech?

options.B: They are replaced by commas
options.C: They are removed

questions.explanation: Quotation marks are removed in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to the comma separating the reporting clause and quotation in indirect speech?

options.B: It is normally removed
options.C: It is replaced by a semicolon
options.D: It is replaced by a colon

questions.explanation: The comma is normally removed when the sentence is recast as an indirect statement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What conjunction is commonly used to introduce reported statements after said, told or explained?

options.B: Whether
options.C: That

questions.explanation: That is commonly used to introduce reported statements after said, told or explained, but it can often be omitted in ordinary English.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to pronouns in indirect speech?

options.A: They are always changed to third person
options.B: They are changed according to the original speaker, listener and reporting context
options.C: They are never changed
options.D: They are always changed to first person

questions.explanation: Change pronouns according to the original speaker, listener and reporting context. Do not change them mechanically without identifying their reference.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to time and place expressions in indirect speech?

options.B: They may change if the reporting situation is at a different time or place
options.C: They are always removed
options.D: They are always changed to past tense

questions.explanation: Time and place expressions may change if the reporting situation is at a different time or place: now → then; here → there; today → that day.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to word order in reported questions?

options.B: Statement word order is used: subject before verb
options.C: The auxiliary do/does/did is retained
options.D: The question mark is always retained

questions.explanation: Use statement word order: subject before verb. Do not retain question inversion or the auxiliary do/does/did.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to question marks and exclamation marks in indirect speech?

options.B: They are generally replaced by a full stop
options.C: They are replaced by commas

questions.explanation: Question marks and exclamation marks are generally replaced by a full stop in an indirect statement, unless the whole reported sentence is itself a question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Simple present tense in direct speech changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Simple past
options.C: Present perfect

questions.explanation: Simple present changes to simple past: "I work." → He said he worked.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Present continuous tense in direct speech changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Present perfect
options.C: Past perfect

questions.explanation: Present continuous changes to past continuous: "I am working." → He said he was working.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Present perfect tense in direct speech changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Past perfect
options.C: Simple past

questions.explanation: Present perfect changes to past perfect: "I have worked." → He said he had worked.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Present perfect continuous tense in direct speech changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Past continuous
options.C: Past perfect continuous

questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous changes to past perfect continuous: "I have been working." → He said he had been working.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Simple past tense in direct speech changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Past continuous
options.C: Past perfect

questions.explanation: Simple past changes to past perfect: "I worked." → He said he had worked.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Past continuous tense in direct speech often changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Past perfect continuous
options.C: Simple past

questions.explanation: Past continuous often changes to past perfect continuous: "I was working." → He said he had been working.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Past perfect tense in direct speech changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Simple past
options.C: No change

questions.explanation: Past perfect normally remains past perfect (no change): "I had worked." → He said he had worked.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Past perfect continuous tense in direct speech changes to which tense in indirect speech?

options.B: No change
options.C: Past continuous

questions.explanation: Past perfect continuous normally remains past perfect continuous (no change): "I had been working." → He said he had been working.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Will in direct speech changes to which modal in indirect speech?

options.B: Would
options.C: Could

questions.explanation: Will changes to would: "I will come." → He said he would come.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Shall (future sense) in direct speech often changes to which modal in indirect speech?

options.B: Would
options.C: Could

questions.explanation: Shall (future sense) often changes to would: "I shall return." → He said he would return.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can in direct speech changes to which modal in indirect speech?

options.B: Could
options.C: Might

questions.explanation: Can changes to could: "I can swim." → He said he could swim.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: May in direct speech changes to which modal in indirect speech?

options.B: Might
options.C: Could

questions.explanation: May changes to might: "I may come." → He said he might come.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Must expressing obligation in direct speech often changes to which form in indirect speech?

options.B: Had to
options.C: Would

questions.explanation: Must expressing obligation often becomes had to: "I must go." → He said he had to go.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does simple past always change to past perfect in indirect speech?

options.B: No, in traditional exam transformations it commonly changes, but in natural reporting past simple may remain when time sequence is clear
options.C: No, it changes to present perfect

questions.explanation: In traditional exam transformations, simple past commonly changes to past perfect when the reporting verb is past. In natural reporting, past simple may remain when the time sequence is clear or the event is still relevant.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does past perfect change in indirect speech?

options.A: Yes, it changes to past perfect continuous
options.B: Yes, it changes to simple past
options.C: No, past perfect normally remains past perfect
options.D: Yes, it changes to present perfect

questions.explanation: Past perfect normally remains past perfect in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does can always change to could in indirect speech?

options.B: Usually yes, but if the ability still exists and context supports it, can may sometimes remain
options.C: No, it changes to might

questions.explanation: Can usually changes to could when the reporting verb is past. If the ability still exists and the context supports it, can may sometimes remain.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does must always change to had to in indirect speech?

options.B: No, must expressing logical deduction or a continuing rule may remain must
options.C: No, it changes to should

questions.explanation: Must expressing past obligation often becomes had to. Must expressing logical deduction or a continuing rule may remain must, depending on meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to should, would, could and might in indirect speech?

options.B: They normally remain unchanged
options.C: They change to had to forms

questions.explanation: Should, would, could and might normally remain unchanged because they are already modal past forms or do not have a regular backshifted equivalent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to ought to in indirect speech?

options.A: It changes to ought to have
options.B: It usually remains ought to
options.C: It changes to should

questions.explanation: Ought to usually remains ought to in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to used to in indirect speech?

options.B: It generally remains used to
options.C: It changes to had used to
options.D: It changes to would use to

questions.explanation: Used to generally remains used to in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to needn't in indirect speech?

options.B: It always changes to didn't have to
options.C: It may remain needn't or change to didn't have to depending on meaning

questions.explanation: Needn't may remain needn't or change to didn't have to, depending on whether the meaning is absence of necessity or a past lack of obligation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is tense backshift normally not required?

options.A: When the reporting verb is in the past
options.B: When the reporting verb is in the present or future, or the reported fact is a universal truth, or information is still true/relevant
options.C: When the sentence is a question
options.D: When the sentence is a command

questions.explanation: Tense backshift is normally not required when the reporting verb is in the present or future, when the reported fact is a universal truth, or when the information is still true/relevant and the speaker chooses to retain the original tense.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to tense when the reporting verb is in the present?

options.B: It normally remains unchanged
options.C: It changes to present perfect

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the present, the tense in the reported clause normally remains unchanged: "She says, 'I am tired'" → She says that she is tired.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to tense when the reporting verb is in the future?

options.B: It normally remains unchanged
options.C: It changes to future perfect

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the future, the tense in the reported clause normally remains unchanged: "He will say, 'I need help'" → He will say that he needs help.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to a universal truth in indirect speech?

options.B: It normally remains in the present tense
options.C: It changes to past perfect

questions.explanation: A universal truth normally remains in the present tense: "The teacher said, 'The Earth revolves around the Sun'" → The teacher said that the Earth revolves around the Sun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to a scientific fact in indirect speech?

options.A: It always changes to past tense
options.B: It normally remains in the present if it is still accepted as true
options.C: It changes to past perfect
options.D: It is converted to a question

questions.explanation: A scientific fact normally remains in the present if it is still accepted as true: "He said, 'Water boils at 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure'" → He said that water boils at 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a fact that is still true remain in the present tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Yes, if the reporter wishes to preserve that fact
options.C: Only for scientific facts
options.D: Only when the reporting verb is present

questions.explanation: Yes. Example: "She said, 'I live in Bengaluru'" → She said that she lives in Bengaluru, if she still lives there and the reporter wishes to preserve that fact.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can backshift still be used for a fact that remains true?

options.B: Only for universal truths
options.C: Yes, backshift may be used to place the statement in the past reporting perspective
options.D: Only when the reporting verb is in the future

questions.explanation: Yes. Backshift may be used to place the statement in the past reporting perspective. Context and intended meaning determine the natural choice.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the basic rule for changing first-person pronouns in indirect speech?

options.A: They always change to third person
options.B: They generally change according to the subject/speaker of the reporting clause
options.C: They never change
options.D: They change according to the listener

questions.explanation: First-person pronouns (I, we, me, us, my, our) generally change according to the subject/speaker of the reporting clause: "Ravi said, 'I am ready'" → Ravi said that he was ready.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the basic rule for changing second-person pronouns in indirect speech?

options.A: They always change to first person
options.B: They change according to the person addressed in the original speech
options.C: They never change
options.D: They always change to third person

questions.explanation: Second-person pronouns (you, your) change according to the person addressed in the original speech: "Ravi said to me, 'You are late'" → Ravi told me that I was late.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to third-person pronouns in indirect speech?

options.A: They always change to first person
options.B: They generally remain the same, unless the reference requires clarification
options.C: They always change to second person

questions.explanation: Third-person pronouns (he, she, it, they and their forms) generally remain the same, unless the reference requires clarification.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Do pronouns always change in the same way in indirect speech?

options.B: No, they depend on who spoke, who was addressed and who is being referred to
options.C: Yes, always first to third person

questions.explanation: No. Identify who spoke, who was addressed and who is being referred to. Pronouns depend on the reporting context.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "She said to me, 'I know you'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: She told me that she knew me.
options.B: She said me that I knew her.
options.C: She told that she knows me.
options.D: She said to me that I know her.

questions.explanation: She told me that she knew me. (I → she; you → me; know → knew)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "The boys said, 'We are ready'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: The boys said that we were ready.
options.B: The boys said that they were ready.
options.C: The boys said that they are ready.
options.D: The boys told that they were ready.

questions.explanation: The boys said that they were ready. (We → they; are → were)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "I said to Ravi, 'You are wrong'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: I told Ravi that he was wrong.
options.B: I said Ravi that you were wrong.
options.C: I told Ravi that I was wrong.
options.D: I said to Ravi that you are wrong.

questions.explanation: I told Ravi that he was wrong. (You → he; are → was)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'now'?

options.B: That day
options.C: The previous day

questions.explanation: Now commonly becomes then / at that time in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'today'?

options.B: That day
options.C: The next day

questions.explanation: Today commonly becomes that day in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'tonight'?

options.B: The previous night
options.C: The following night

questions.explanation: Tonight commonly becomes that night in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'yesterday'?

options.B: The previous day / the day before
options.C: The next day

questions.explanation: Yesterday commonly becomes the previous day / the day before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'tomorrow'?

options.B: That day
options.C: The next day / the following day

questions.explanation: Tomorrow commonly becomes the next day / the following day in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'the day before yesterday'?

options.B: The previous day
options.C: Two days later

questions.explanation: The day before yesterday commonly becomes two days before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'the day after tomorrow'?

options.B: In two days' time / two days later
options.C: The next day

questions.explanation: The day after tomorrow commonly becomes in two days' time / two days later in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'last night'?

options.B: The previous night / the night before
options.C: The following night

questions.explanation: Last night commonly becomes the previous night / the night before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'last week/month/year'?

options.B: That week/month/year
options.C: The previous week/month/year

questions.explanation: Last week/month/year commonly becomes the previous week/month/year in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'next week/month/year'?

options.B: The following week/month/year
options.C: That week/month/year

questions.explanation: Next week/month/year commonly becomes the following week/month/year in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'ago'?

options.B: After
options.C: Later

questions.explanation: Ago commonly becomes before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'here'?

options.B: There
options.C: Then

questions.explanation: Here commonly becomes there in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'this'?

options.B: That
options.C: Those

questions.explanation: This commonly becomes that in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'these'?

options.B: That
options.C: Those

questions.explanation: These commonly becomes those in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'come'?

options.B: Go (often, if viewpoint changes)
options.C: Came

questions.explanation: Come often becomes go if the viewpoint changes in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'bring'?

options.B: Take (often, if viewpoint changes)
options.C: Bringing

questions.explanation: Bring often becomes take if the viewpoint changes in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Do time and place expressions always have to change in indirect speech?

options.B: No, they change only when the reporting context has changed
options.C: Only for questions

questions.explanation: No. They change only when the reporting context has changed. If the report is made at the same time and place, words such as today, tomorrow or here may remain.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why does 'here' sometimes become 'there' in indirect speech?

options.B: Because the reporter may be speaking from a different place from the original speaker
options.C: Because here is always a pronoun
options.D: Because here is a question word

questions.explanation: Here sometimes becomes there because the reporter may be speaking from a different place from the original speaker.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why does 'this' sometimes become 'that' in indirect speech?

options.B: Because the demonstrative reference may be farther from the reporter or the original context may have changed
options.C: Because this is a verb

questions.explanation: This sometimes becomes that because the demonstrative reference may be farther from the reporter or the original context may have changed.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why can 'come' change to 'go' in indirect speech?

options.A: It is an automatic tense rule
options.B: The verb may change to match the reporter's viewpoint and destination
options.C: Because come is always past tense

questions.explanation: The verb may change to match the reporter's viewpoint and destination. It is not an automatic tense rule.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are affirmative statements changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Use said/told + (that) + subject + verb in the appropriate tense
options.B: Use asked + if + subject + verb
options.C: Use ordered + object + to-infinitive

questions.explanation: Use said/told + (that) + subject + verb in the appropriate tense: "He said, 'I am happy'" → He said (that) he was happy.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are negative statements changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Remove not from the reported clause
options.B: Retain not in the reported clause and apply appropriate tense/pronoun changes
options.C: Change not to no
options.D: Add do not before the verb

questions.explanation: Retain not in the reported clause and apply the appropriate tense/pronoun changes: "She said, 'I do not agree'" → She said that she did not agree.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between said and told?

options.A: Say is used with a personal object; tell is used without
options.B: Say is normally used without a personal object; tell normally takes a personal object
options.C: They are always interchangeable
options.D: Tell is only used for questions

questions.explanation: Say is normally used without a personal object: "He said that..." Tell normally takes a personal object: "He told me that..."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is "He told that he was ill" correct?

options.B: No, use "He said that he was ill" or "He told me that he was ill"
options.C: Yes, but only in informal speech
options.D: No, use "He told to me that he was ill"

questions.explanation: No, not in standard usage. Say "He said that he was ill" or "He told me that he was ill."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can 'that' be omitted after said or told in reported statements?

options.B: Yes, that is often optional in ordinary reported statements
options.C: Only for negative statements

questions.explanation: Yes, that is often optional in ordinary reported statements: "She said (that) she was ready."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are yes/no questions changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Use asked/wanted to know + if or whether + subject + verb in statement order
options.B: Use asked + wh-word + subject + verb
options.C: Use told + object + to-infinitive
options.D: Retain the question mark and inversion

questions.explanation: Use asked/wanted to know + if or whether + subject + verb in statement order: "He asked, 'Are you ready?'" → He asked if I was ready.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which conjunctions introduce reported yes/no questions?

options.B: If and whether
options.C: Who and whom

questions.explanation: If and whether introduce reported yes/no questions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is the question mark retained in a reported yes/no question?

options.B: Normally no, because the reported clause is part of a statement
options.C: Only for negative questions

questions.explanation: Normally no, because the reported clause is part of a statement: "She asked whether I was ready."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is do/does/did used in the reported question clause in indirect speech?

options.B: Normally no; remove question inversion and use statement word order
options.C: Only for yes/no questions

questions.explanation: Normally no. Remove question inversion and use statement word order: "Did he come?" → She asked whether he had come.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "He said to me, 'Do you know her?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: He asked me if I knew her.
options.B: He said me if I know her.
options.C: He told me that I knew her.
options.D: He asked me that did I know her.

questions.explanation: He asked me if I knew her. (said to → asked; do you know → I knew; if introduces the reported yes/no question)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "She asked, 'Have you finished?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: She asked if I have finished.
options.B: She asked whether I had finished.
options.C: She asked that I had finished.
options.D: She told me whether I finished.

questions.explanation: She asked whether I had finished. (present perfect → past perfect; whether introduces the reported yes/no question)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can 'whether' be followed by 'or not' in indirect speech?

options.B: Yes: "He asked whether or not I agreed" or "He asked whether I agreed or not"
options.C: Only in formal writing
options.D: Only with yes/no questions in the present tense

questions.explanation: Yes: "He asked whether or not I agreed"; or "He asked whether I agreed or not."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are wh-questions changed into indirect speech?

options.B: Retain the wh-word and use statement word order
options.C: Use that + subject + verb

questions.explanation: Retain the wh-word (who, what, when, where, why, how, which) and use statement word order: "Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is if or whether used with a wh-question in indirect speech?

options.B: Normally no; the wh-word itself introduces the reported question
options.C: Only for negative questions

questions.explanation: Normally no. The wh-word itself introduces the reported question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does the reported wh-question end with a question mark when embedded in a statement?

options.B: Usually no
options.C: Only for formal writing

questions.explanation: Usually no when it is embedded in a statement: "She asked where I lived."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "He asked me, 'What are you doing?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: He asked me what I was doing.
options.B: He asked me what was I doing.
options.C: He asked me that what I was doing.
options.D: He told me what I was doing.

questions.explanation: He asked me what I was doing. (statement word order: subject before verb; present continuous → past continuous)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "The teacher asked, 'Why are you late?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: The teacher asked why I was late.
options.B: The teacher asked why was I late.
options.C: The teacher asked that why I was late.
options.D: The teacher told why I was late.

questions.explanation: The teacher asked why I was late. (wh-word retained; statement word order; present → past)

questions.subject: English

questions.question: Change into indirect speech: The officer said to the man, "Show me your identity card."

options.A: The officer ordered the man to show him his identity card.
options.B: The officer ordered the man to show me his identity card.
options.C: The officer told the man that show him his identity card.
options.D: The officer ordered the man to show his identity card to me.

questions.explanation: The officer ordered the man to show him his identity card. (me → him; your → his; command → ordered + object + to-infinitive)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, "Please wait here."

options.A: She requested me to wait there.
options.B: She requested me to wait here.
options.C: She told me to wait there.

questions.explanation: She requested me to wait there. (request → requested + object + to-infinitive; here → there)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: The doctor said to him, "Take this medicine."

options.B: The doctor advised him to take this medicine.
options.C: The doctor told him to take this medicine.

questions.explanation: The doctor advised him to take that medicine. (advice → advised + object + to-infinitive; this → that)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: He said, "Alas! I have lost my purse."

options.A: He exclaimed with sorrow that he had lost his purse.
options.B: He exclaimed with joy that he had lost his purse.
options.C: He said with sorrow that he has lost his purse.
options.D: He exclaimed with sorrow that he has lost his purse.

questions.explanation: He exclaimed with sorrow that he had lost his purse. (Alas! → exclaimed with sorrow; I → he; my → his; present perfect → past perfect)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: She said, "Hurrah! We have won the match."

options.A: She exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
options.B: She exclaimed with joy that we had won the match.
options.C: She exclaimed with sorrow that they had won the match.
options.D: She said with joy that they have won the match.

questions.explanation: She exclaimed with joy that they had won the match. (Hurrah! → exclaimed with joy; we → they; present perfect → past perfect)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: He said, "Let us go for a walk."

options.A: He suggested that they should go for a walk / He suggested going for a walk.
options.B: He suggested that we should go for a walk.
options.C: He said that let us go for a walk.
options.D: He ordered them to go for a walk.

questions.explanation: He suggested that they should go for a walk / He suggested going for a walk. (Let us → suggested + that-clause with should / suggested + gerund; us → they)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: She said, "I may come today."

options.A: She said that she might come that day.
options.B: She said that she may come today.
options.C: She said that she might come today.
options.D: She told that she might come that day.

questions.explanation: She said that she might come that day. (may → might; today → that day)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: He said, "I must finish this work." (For obligation.)

options.A: He said that he had to finish that work.
options.B: He said that he must finish that work.
options.C: He said that he had to finish this work.
options.D: He told that he had to finish that work.

questions.explanation: He said that he had to finish that work. (must for obligation → had to; this → that)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: The boy said, "Who broke the glass?"

options.A: The boy asked who had broken the glass.
options.B: The boy asked who broke the glass.
options.C: The boy asked who did break the glass.
options.D: The boy asked that who had broken the glass.

questions.explanation: The boy asked who had broken the glass. (who is the subject; no do-support; simple past → past perfect)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: He said to her, "Why are you crying?"

options.A: He asked her why she was crying.
options.B: He asked her why was she crying.
options.C: He told her why she was crying.
options.D: He asked her that why she was crying.

questions.explanation: He asked her why she was crying. (wh-word retained; statement word order; present continuous → past continuous; you → she)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Change into indirect speech: She said, "I do not like coffee."

options.B: She said that she does not like coffee.

options.D: She said that I did not like coffee.

questions.explanation: She said that she did not like coffee. (I → she; do not like → did not like)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of direct speech?

options.A: He said that he was busy.
options.B: He said, "I am busy."
options.C: He told me that he was busy.
options.D: He explained that he was busy.

questions.explanation: Direct speech reports the exact words spoken by a person, usually within quotation marks: He said, "I am busy."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of indirect speech?

options.B: He said that he was busy.
options.C: He said, "I am busy," to me.

questions.explanation: Indirect speech reports the meaning of someone's words without quoting the exact words: He said that he was busy.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a reporting verb?

options.B: Happy
options.C: Asked

questions.explanation: A reporting verb introduces the reported words, such as say, tell, ask, reply, explain, request, order, advise and suggest. Asked is a reporting verb.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In "She said that she was tired," what is the reporting clause?

options.B: She said
options.C: she was tired

questions.explanation: The reporting clause identifies the speaker or reporting act: "She said" is the reporting clause in "She said that she was tired."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In "She said that she was tired," what is the reported clause?

options.B: that she was tired
options.C: She said that

questions.explanation: The reported clause contains the words or meaning being reported: "that she was tired" in "She said that she was tired."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which punctuation is typically used around the exact spoken words in direct speech?

options.B: Quotation marks
options.C: Brackets

questions.explanation: Quotation marks are used around the exact spoken words in direct speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the core principle of reported speech?

options.A: Change the meaning of the original sentence
options.B: Change the reporting structure while preserving the original meaning
options.C: Always use quotation marks
options.D: Always change pronouns to third person

questions.explanation: Core principle: In reported speech, change the reporting structure while preserving the original meaning. Changes in tense, pronouns, demonstratives and time/place expressions depend on the reporting verb, context and whether the information is still true or relevant.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What does 'backshift' refer to in indirect speech?

options.B: The usual movement of the reported verb to a past form when the reporting verb is in the past
options.C: Removing quotation marks

questions.explanation: Backshift is the usual movement of the reported verb to a past form when the reporting verb is in the past: present simple → past simple; present perfect → past perfect.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following modal verbs does NOT have a regular backshifted equivalent and normally remains unchanged?

options.B: Can
options.C: Should

questions.explanation: Should, would, could and might normally remain unchanged because they are already modal past forms or do not have a regular backshifted equivalent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following modal verbs does NOT have a regular backshifted equivalent and normally remains unchanged?

options.B: Would
options.C: Can

questions.explanation: Should, would, could and might normally remain unchanged because they are already modal past forms or do not have a regular backshifted equivalent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following modal verbs does NOT have a regular backshifted equivalent and normally remains unchanged?

options.B: May
options.C: Could

questions.explanation: Should, would, could and might normally remain unchanged because they are already modal past forms or do not have a regular backshifted equivalent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following modal verbs does NOT have a regular backshifted equivalent and normally remains unchanged?

options.B: Can
options.C: May

questions.explanation: Should, would, could and might normally remain unchanged because they are already modal past forms or do not have a regular backshifted equivalent.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to 'ought to' in indirect speech?

options.A: It changes to ought to have
options.B: It usually remains ought to
options.C: It changes to should

questions.explanation: Ought to usually remains ought to in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to 'used to' in indirect speech?

options.B: It generally remains used to
options.C: It changes to had used to
options.D: It changes to would use to

questions.explanation: Used to generally remains used to in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to 'needn't' in indirect speech?

options.B: It always changes to didn't have to
options.C: It may remain needn't or change to didn't have to depending on meaning

questions.explanation: Needn't may remain needn't or change to didn't have to, depending on whether the meaning is absence of necessity or a past lack of obligation.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does 'must' always change to 'had to' in indirect speech?

options.B: No, must expressing logical deduction or a continuing rule may remain must
options.C: No, it changes to should

questions.explanation: Must expressing past obligation often becomes had to. Must expressing logical deduction or a continuing rule may remain must, depending on meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does 'can' always change to 'could' in indirect speech?

options.B: Usually yes, but if the ability still exists and context supports it, can may sometimes remain
options.C: No, it changes to might

questions.explanation: Can usually changes to could when the reporting verb is past. If the ability still exists and the context supports it, can may sometimes remain.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does simple past always change to past perfect in indirect speech?

options.B: No, in traditional exam transformations it commonly changes, but in natural reporting past simple may remain when time sequence is clear
options.C: No, it changes to present perfect

questions.explanation: In traditional exam transformations, simple past commonly changes to past perfect when the reporting verb is past. In natural reporting, past simple may remain when the time sequence is clear or the event is still relevant.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does past perfect change in indirect speech?

options.A: Yes, it changes to past perfect continuous
options.B: Yes, it changes to simple past
options.C: No, past perfect normally remains past perfect
options.D: Yes, it changes to present perfect

questions.explanation: Past perfect normally remains past perfect in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When is tense backshift normally not required?

options.A: When the reporting verb is in the past
options.B: When the reporting verb is in the present or future, or the reported fact is a universal truth, or information is still true/relevant
options.C: When the sentence is a question
options.D: When the sentence is a command

questions.explanation: Tense backshift is normally not required when the reporting verb is in the present or future, when the reported fact is a universal truth, or when the information is still true/relevant and the speaker chooses to retain the original tense.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to tense when the reporting verb is in the present?

options.B: It normally remains unchanged
options.C: It changes to present perfect

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the present, the tense in the reported clause normally remains unchanged: "She says, 'I am tired'" → She says that she is tired.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to tense when the reporting verb is in the future?

options.B: It normally remains unchanged
options.C: It changes to future perfect

questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is in the future, the tense in the reported clause normally remains unchanged: "He will say, 'I need help'" → He will say that he needs help.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to a universal truth in indirect speech?

options.B: It normally remains in the present tense
options.C: It changes to past perfect

questions.explanation: A universal truth normally remains in the present tense: "The teacher said, 'The Earth revolves around the Sun'" → The teacher said that the Earth revolves around the Sun.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to a scientific fact in indirect speech?

options.A: It always changes to past tense
options.B: It normally remains in the present if it is still accepted as true
options.C: It changes to past perfect
options.D: It is converted to a question

questions.explanation: A scientific fact normally remains in the present if it is still accepted as true: "He said, 'Water boils at 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure'" → He said that water boils at 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can a fact that is still true remain in the present tense in indirect speech?

options.B: Yes, if the reporter wishes to preserve that fact
options.C: Only for scientific facts
options.D: Only when the reporting verb is present

questions.explanation: Yes. Example: "She said, 'I live in Bengaluru'" → She said that she lives in Bengaluru, if she still lives there and the reporter wishes to preserve that fact.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can backshift still be used for a fact that remains true?

options.B: Only for universal truths
options.C: Yes, backshift may be used to place the statement in the past reporting perspective
options.D: Only when the reporting verb is in the future

questions.explanation: Yes. Backshift may be used to place the statement in the past reporting perspective. Context and intended meaning determine the natural choice.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the basic rule for changing first-person pronouns in indirect speech?

options.A: They always change to third person
options.B: They generally change according to the subject/speaker of the reporting clause
options.C: They never change
options.D: They change according to the listener

questions.explanation: First-person pronouns (I, we, me, us, my, our) generally change according to the subject/speaker of the reporting clause: "Ravi said, 'I am ready'" → Ravi said that he was ready.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the basic rule for changing second-person pronouns in indirect speech?

options.A: They always change to first person
options.B: They change according to the person addressed in the original speech
options.C: They never change
options.D: They always change to third person

questions.explanation: Second-person pronouns (you, your) change according to the person addressed in the original speech: "Ravi said to me, 'You are late'" → Ravi told me that I was late.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens to third-person pronouns in indirect speech?

options.A: They always change to first person
options.B: They generally remain the same, unless the reference requires clarification
options.C: They always change to second person

questions.explanation: Third-person pronouns (he, she, it, they and their forms) generally remain the same, unless the reference requires clarification.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Do pronouns always change in the same way in indirect speech?

options.B: No, they depend on who spoke, who was addressed and who is being referred to
options.C: Yes, always first to third person

questions.explanation: No. Identify who spoke, who was addressed and who is being referred to. Pronouns depend on the reporting context.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "She said to me, 'I know you'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: She told me that she knew me.
options.B: She said me that I knew her.
options.C: She told that she knows me.
options.D: She said to me that I know her.

questions.explanation: She told me that she knew me. (I → she; you → me; know → knew)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "The boys said, 'We are ready'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: The boys said that we were ready.
options.B: The boys said that they were ready.
options.C: The boys said that they are ready.
options.D: The boys told that they were ready.

questions.explanation: The boys said that they were ready. (We → they; are → were)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "I said to Ravi, 'You are wrong'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: I told Ravi that he was wrong.
options.B: I said Ravi that you were wrong.
options.C: I told Ravi that I was wrong.
options.D: I said to Ravi that you are wrong.

questions.explanation: I told Ravi that he was wrong. (You → he; are → was)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'now'?

options.B: That day
options.C: The previous day

questions.explanation: Now commonly becomes then / at that time in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'today'?

options.B: That day
options.C: The next day

questions.explanation: Today commonly becomes that day in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'tonight'?

options.B: The previous night
options.C: The following night

questions.explanation: Tonight commonly becomes that night in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'yesterday'?

options.B: The previous day / the day before
options.C: The next day

questions.explanation: Yesterday commonly becomes the previous day / the day before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'tomorrow'?

options.B: That day
options.C: The next day / the following day

questions.explanation: Tomorrow commonly becomes the next day / the following day in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'the day before yesterday'?

options.B: The previous day
options.C: Two days later

questions.explanation: The day before yesterday commonly becomes two days before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'the day after tomorrow'?

options.B: In two days' time / two days later
options.C: The next day

questions.explanation: The day after tomorrow commonly becomes in two days' time / two days later in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'last night'?

options.B: The previous night / the night before
options.C: The following night

questions.explanation: Last night commonly becomes the previous night / the night before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'last week/month/year'?

options.B: That week/month/year
options.C: The previous week/month/year

questions.explanation: Last week/month/year commonly becomes the previous week/month/year in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'next week/month/year'?

options.B: The following week/month/year
options.C: That week/month/year

questions.explanation: Next week/month/year commonly becomes the following week/month/year in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'ago'?

options.B: After
options.C: Later

questions.explanation: Ago commonly becomes before in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'here'?

options.B: There
options.C: Then

questions.explanation: Here commonly becomes there in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'this'?

options.B: That
options.C: Those

questions.explanation: This commonly becomes that in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'these'?

options.B: That
options.C: Those

questions.explanation: These commonly becomes those in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'come'?

options.B: Go (often, if viewpoint changes)
options.C: Came

questions.explanation: Come often becomes go if the viewpoint changes in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the common indirect form of 'bring'?

options.B: Take (often, if viewpoint changes)
options.C: Bringing

questions.explanation: Bring often becomes take if the viewpoint changes in indirect speech.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Do time and place expressions always have to change in indirect speech?

options.B: No, they change only when the reporting context has changed
options.C: Only for questions

questions.explanation: No. They change only when the reporting context has changed. If the report is made at the same time and place, words such as today, tomorrow or here may remain.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why does 'here' sometimes become 'there' in indirect speech?

options.B: Because the reporter may be speaking from a different place from the original speaker
options.C: Because here is always a pronoun
options.D: Because here is a question word

questions.explanation: Here sometimes becomes there because the reporter may be speaking from a different place from the original speaker.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why does 'this' sometimes become 'that' in indirect speech?

options.B: Because the demonstrative reference may be farther from the reporter or the original context may have changed
options.C: Because this is a verb

questions.explanation: This sometimes becomes that because the demonstrative reference may be farther from the reporter or the original context may have changed.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why can 'come' change to 'go' in indirect speech?

options.A: It is an automatic tense rule
options.B: The verb may change to match the reporter's viewpoint and destination
options.C: Because come is always past tense

questions.explanation: The verb may change to match the reporter's viewpoint and destination. It is not an automatic tense rule.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are affirmative statements changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Use said/told + (that) + subject + verb in the appropriate tense
options.B: Use asked + if + subject + verb
options.C: Use ordered + object + to-infinitive

questions.explanation: Use said/told + (that) + subject + verb in the appropriate tense: "He said, 'I am happy'" → He said (that) he was happy.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are negative statements changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Remove not from the reported clause
options.B: Retain not in the reported clause and apply appropriate tense/pronoun changes
options.C: Change not to no
options.D: Add do not before the verb

questions.explanation: Retain not in the reported clause and apply the appropriate tense/pronoun changes: "She said, 'I do not agree'" → She said that she did not agree.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the difference between said and told?

options.A: Say is used with a personal object; tell is used without
options.B: Say is normally used without a personal object; tell normally takes a personal object
options.C: They are always interchangeable
options.D: Tell is only used for questions

questions.explanation: Say is normally used without a personal object: "He said that..." Tell normally takes a personal object: "He told me that..."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is "He told that he was ill" correct?

options.B: No, use "He said that he was ill" or "He told me that he was ill"
options.C: Yes, but only in informal speech
options.D: No, use "He told to me that he was ill"

questions.explanation: No, not in standard usage. Say "He said that he was ill" or "He told me that he was ill."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can 'that' be omitted after said or told in reported statements?

options.B: Yes, that is often optional in ordinary reported statements
options.C: Only for negative statements

questions.explanation: Yes, that is often optional in ordinary reported statements: "She said (that) she was ready."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are yes/no questions changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Use asked/wanted to know + if or whether + subject + verb in statement order
options.B: Use asked + wh-word + subject + verb
options.C: Use told + object + to-infinitive
options.D: Retain the question mark and inversion

questions.explanation: Use asked/wanted to know + if or whether + subject + verb in statement order: "He asked, 'Are you ready?'" → He asked if I was ready.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which conjunctions introduce reported yes/no questions?

options.B: If and whether
options.C: Who and whom

questions.explanation: If and whether introduce reported yes/no questions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is the question mark retained in a reported yes/no question?

options.B: Normally no, because the reported clause is part of a statement
options.C: Only for negative questions

questions.explanation: Normally no, because the reported clause is part of a statement: "She asked whether I was ready."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is do/does/did used in the reported question clause in indirect speech?

options.B: Normally no; remove question inversion and use statement word order
options.C: Only for yes/no questions

questions.explanation: Normally no. Remove question inversion and use statement word order: "Did he come?" → She asked whether he had come.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "He said to me, 'Do you know her?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: He asked me if I knew her.
options.B: He said me if I know her.
options.C: He told me that I knew her.
options.D: He asked me that did I know her.

questions.explanation: He asked me if I knew her. (said to → asked; do you know → I knew; if introduces the reported yes/no question)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "She asked, 'Have you finished?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: She asked if I have finished.
options.B: She asked whether I had finished.
options.C: She asked that I had finished.
options.D: She told me whether I finished.

questions.explanation: She asked whether I had finished. (present perfect → past perfect; whether introduces the reported yes/no question)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Can 'whether' be followed by 'or not' in indirect speech?

options.B: Yes: "He asked whether or not I agreed" or "He asked whether I agreed or not"
options.C: Only in formal writing
options.D: Only with yes/no questions in the present tense

questions.explanation: Yes: "He asked whether or not I agreed"; or "He asked whether I agreed or not."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are wh-questions changed into indirect speech?

options.B: Retain the wh-word and use statement word order
options.C: Use that + subject + verb

questions.explanation: Retain the wh-word (who, what, when, where, why, how, which) and use statement word order: "Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Is if or whether used with a wh-question in indirect speech?

options.B: Normally no; the wh-word itself introduces the reported question
options.C: Only for negative questions

questions.explanation: Normally no. The wh-word itself introduces the reported question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Does the reported wh-question end with a question mark when embedded in a statement?

options.B: Usually no
options.C: Only for formal writing

questions.explanation: Usually no when it is embedded in a statement: "She asked where I lived."

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "He asked me, 'What are you doing?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: He asked me what I was doing.
options.B: He asked me what was I doing.
options.C: He asked me that what I was doing.
options.D: He told me what I was doing.

questions.explanation: He asked me what I was doing. (statement word order: subject before verb; present continuous → past continuous)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "The teacher asked, 'Why are you late?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: The teacher asked why I was late.
options.B: The teacher asked why was I late.
options.C: The teacher asked that why I was late.
options.D: The teacher told why I was late.

questions.explanation: The teacher asked why I was late. (wh-word retained; statement word order; present → past)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How is "She asked, 'When will the train arrive?'" changed into indirect speech?

options.A: She asked when the train will arrive.
options.B: She asked when would the train arrive.
options.C: She asked when the train would arrive.
options.D: She asked that when the train would arrive.

questions.explanation: She asked when the train would arrive. (will → would; statement word order)

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What happens when who/what is the subject of the original question in indirect speech?

options.B: The subject order may already be natural; do not insert unnecessary do-support
options.C: Change who to whom always

questions.explanation: The subject order may already be natural: "Who broke the window?" → He asked who had broken the window. Do not insert an unnecessary do-support form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are commands changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Use a suitable reporting verb + object + to-infinitive
options.B: Use asked + if + subject + verb
options.C: Use said + that + clause

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How are negative commands changed into indirect speech?

options.A: Use reporting verb + object + not to + base verb
options.B: Use reporting verb + object + to not + base verb
options.C: Use reporting verb + that + not + clause

questions.explanation: Use reporting verb + object + not to + base verb: "He said, 'Do not touch it'" → He told me not to touch it.

questions.question: Which reporting verbs are used for commands in indirect speech?

options.B: Order, command, instruct, direct and tell
options.C: Suggest, propose, recommend

questions.explanation: Order, command, instruct, direct and tell are used for commands, depending on context.

questions.question: How are polite requests changed into indirect speech?

options.B: Use ask/request + object + to-infinitive
options.C: Use suggest + gerund

questions.explanation: Use ask/request + object + to-infinitive: "She said, 'Please help me'" → She requested me to help her / She asked me to help her.
